scenarios.name: Normal user activity
scenarios.description: Routine logons, document editing, browsing and file reads with no loss events.
scenarios.notes: Baseline true-negative case: any rule firing here is a false positive.

scenarios.name: Legitimate administrative cleanup
scenarios.description: A scheduled disk-cleanup run deleting temp cache files (bulk deletions, benign).
scenarios.notes: Ground truth: the bulk-deletion (AF-003) and work-then-loss (AF-005) DETECTIONS are correct — targets are temp files and the named tool (cleanmgr.exe) is in the execution record, so the report must present them as high-volume but plausibly benign. Detection accuracy is scored on whether the rule fires, not on whether the activity is malicious.

scenarios.name: Forensic artifact deletion
scenarios.description: USN journal records show deletion of an event log, a prefetch artifact and a sensitive document.
alternatives: Log retention policy deleting aged logs

scenarios.name: Audit log clearing
scenarios.description: Security log clear (1102) after an interactive command shell execution.
alternatives: Ordinary administrative shell session followed by a retention task
scenarios.notes: AF-008 fires at reduced severity: the preceding execution (cmd.exe) shares the user/host but is not a documented anti-forensic utility, so support stays low and the report must say a routine shell session explains the pair. AF-005 and pattern D match the same activity→loss sequence.

scenarios.name: Timestamp inconsistency
scenarios.description: One record with modified < created, one with three identical metadata timestamps, and one normal record as a control.
scenarios.notes: The control record must NOT be flagged — demonstrates that not every unusual timestamp is treated as manipulation.

scenarios.name: Filesystem CSV export (parser coverage)
scenarios.description: USN-style CSV export including one intentionally invalid row so rejected-record reporting is exercised end to end.
alternatives: Ordinary application file updates during patching
scenarios.notes: The CSV bytes are generated and imported through the real CSV parser, so the rejection shown in the UI comes from the parser, not a pre-baked table.

scenarios.name: Multiple suspicious actions
scenarios.description: Encoded PowerShell → log access → copy candidate → eviction → log clear → metadata anomaly → removable media transfer.
alternatives: Approved log rotation invoked through the same utilities
Backup/sync tool copying then pruning files

scenarios.name: Incomplete evidence collection
scenarios.description: A 14h48m logging gap while non-log activity continues, plus records with missing timestamps and rejected rows.
alternatives: Evidence acquisition incomplete for the period
Logging disabled or expired by configuration
Host offline / user inactive (weaker here because other artifacts continue)
scenarios.notes: Demonstrates: rejected rows are reported, undated records never get a fake time, and absence of log records is treated as missing coverage, not deletion.

scenarios.name: Clock drift and inconsistent timezones
scenarios.description: Mixed offsets (-05:30, +05:45, UTC), a recorded clock change and preserved raw source strings.
scenarios.notes: Raw source timestamps are preserved next to the normalized UTC value.

scenarios.name: Unrelated events occurring close together
scenarios.description: Four events within 15 seconds across two hosts and two users — high temporal overlap without any shared anchor.
alternatives: Scheduled tasks firing on their own cadence
scenarios.notes: True-positive for AF-001 (the clear IS recorded) but a negative for sequence inference: no chain and no POSSIBLY_CAUSAL edge may be produced, because the events share no user/host/file anchor.

scenarios.name: Mixed benign and suspicious sequences
scenarios.description: Routine work in the morning, then an anti-forensic utility run, log clear, prefetch deletion and a uniform-timestamp anomaly.
alternatives: Approved log rotation invoked through the same utilities
